problem: What is the limit of the sequence ${a}_{n}=\frac{\sqrt{n}}{{log}_{2}⁡n}-1$ for $n>1?$
worked_solution:
Recall that for large values of $n,$ we have

$$
n!≫{e}^{n}≫{n}^{m}≫\operatorname{ln}⁡(n),
$$

where $≫$ means "much greater than," and $m>0.$

We calculate the limit of the sequence as $n$ approaches infinity:

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n}={lim}_{n\to \infty }(\frac{\sqrt{n}}{{log}_{2}⁡n}-1)=-1+{lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt{n}}{{log}_{2}⁡n}
$$

Both the numerator and denominator approach infinity as $n\to \infty .$ However, the numerator is growing much faster than the denominator, and we conclude that

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt{n}}{{log}_{2}⁡n}=\infty .
$$

Hence, 

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }(\frac{\sqrt{n}}{{log}_{2}⁡n}-1)=\infty .
$$

Therefore, the sequence diverges.
